verdict: Do not roll out a 32-hour four-day week to all 300 support staff from Q2 on the strength of the COO's '40% productivity' claim. Instead, start Q2 with a measured pilot: randomly assigned (not volunteer) teams, staggered days off, concurrent control teams, pay terms fixed in advance, and go/no-go rules set before launch. The 40% figure matches two sources. One is a self-rated survey of 60 engineering and design staff at Kestrel (E1). The other is Microsoft Japan's one-month, year-on-year sales-per-employee figure of 39.9% (E10, E22); no comparison group is described for it, so 'uncontrolled' is an inference. Neither is a controlled measure of total output. The strongest source is the Nordvik et al. cluster-RCT summary (E2). It reports pooled team output of -2% (95% CI -7% to +3%) across 112 teams, including non-support billable work. The size of the hours cut is not stated, and our arithmetic assumes 40 to 32 hours (E5). Output for the customer-service subgroup is not reported. At 300 staff the -7% lower bound is about 21 FTE-equivalents of throughput (K13). In the 31 customer-service teams, first-response time was 11% slower (95% CI +4% to +18%) unless schedules were staggered (E3). Nordvik also reports wellbeing up 0.4 SD and annualised voluntary attrition of 9.1% vs 13.0% (E4). The summary gives no confidence intervals or significance tests for these, does not label the arms, and does not say whether the wellbeing figure compares arms or is a before-and-after change (E18). They are possible benefits of unknown reliability, not established effects. None of the four supplied sources states pay terms (E18, E19). The external trials with positive wellbeing results ran at full pay (E20, E23, E24, E11). At full pay, cost per paid hour rises 25% (K12), and that is the main cost line. At reduced pay, the benefits may not carry over. Whether a full rollout would pay off cannot be determined without three things: the org's SLA headroom, coverage hours, attrition, cost per hire and utilisation (E17); its intended pay terms; and independent confirmation of the Nordvik paper (E8). A pilot produces the missing service and cost evidence while capping risk. The evidence does not justify a full rollout, and it does not rule the idea out either, so not proceeding is not clearly supported.

criteriaAssessments.assessment: Evidence quality varies widely. Nordvik (E2, E3, E4) is the only randomised, objectively measured source with a customer-service subgroup, so it should dominate. However, it is known only from a short summary that omits pay terms, arm labels and uncertainty for wellbeing and attrition (E18), and its existence could not be externally verified (E8). Kestrel (E1) is a self-rated, uncontrolled company blog about 60 engineering and design staff. Workforce Pulse (E6) measures hypothetical intent, not an effect. Varmland (E7) is a milder 40-to-36-hour change in a municipal setting, with service judged by management, and it is unverified (E9). External sources (E10 to E15, E20 to E24) are non-randomised and rest on search summaries only. Fan, Schor et al. is reported in Nature Human Behaviour across several domains (E21); peer review is inferred from the venue, not confirmed. Contradictions in the packet, and how each is handled: (1) Kestrel's +40% self-rated figure and Microsoft Japan's 39.9% sales-per-employee figure vs Nordvik's -2% objective output (E1, E10, E22 vs E2). Nordvik is preferred: it is randomised, measures output objectively, and is closer to support work. The other two measure different things. (2) UK pilot continuation and durability (E12) vs Nordvik (E2). These are not in direct conflict: E12 concerns employer retention of the policy and self-reported wellbeing, not objective output. (3) Fan sample sizes, 290 controls (E11) vs 285 (E21). The more recent, corroborated E21 is preferred, and the difference does not matter here. (4) South Cambridgeshire contact-centre call answering (E15) vs Nordvik's response-time penalty (E3) and the ministerial concern about fewer calls answered (E24). This is unresolved: the South Cambs rota design is undocumented (E25), and E15 and E24 may refer to different metrics or periods.
criteriaAssessments.mechanisms: Self-rated productivity after a desired policy change is inflated by expectancy, gratitude and selection effects, and without a control group secular trends cannot be separated from the treatment. Year-on-year sales ratios are confounded by seasonality and product cycles (E22). Randomising at team level removes selection bias, and objective ticket counts remove reporting bias. That is why E2 outranks E1 despite their contradictory headlines. Transfer to support work also depends on how far the work is coverage-bound: engineering output can be shifted in time, but live queue response cannot.
strengths: One randomised trial with objective output and a support-specific response-time subgroup (E2, E3)

Independent, non-randomised evidence reported in Nature Human Behaviour points the same way on wellbeing (E21, E11), and there is some self-reported evidence that the effect lasts to about 12 months (E12)
Several analogues agree on the coverage-cost mechanism (E7, E13, E14)
weaknesses: Nordvik is an unverified working paper known only from a short summary. Peer review, pre-registration, contamination checks and pay terms are unknown, and there is no uncertainty given for wellbeing or attrition (E2, E8, E18)
Kestrel, Workforce Pulse and Varmland are weak or transfer poorly (E1, E6, E7, E9)
All web-sourced evidence rests on search summaries because every page fetch failed (E10, E11, E12, E13, E15, E20 to E24)

criteriaAssessments.assessment: The pooled estimate is that total team output stays roughly flat: -2%, with a 95% CI of -7% to +3% (E2). Two caveats apply. First, Nordvik's baseline hours are not stated. If hours fell from 40 to 32 (an assumed 20% cut, K5), output per paid hour rose by about 22.5% (K1), with a range of about +16% to +29% across the CI (K3, K4). Second, the -2% is pooled across 112 teams, and outcomes include non-support billable output. No customer-service subgroup output figure is reported (E2). The subgroup's +11% first-response penalty (E3) suggests support teams may sit at the worse end of the range, but that cannot be confirmed. At the -7% lower bound, a 300-person org would lose about 21 FTE-equivalents of throughput (K13). No source in the packet shows a controlled 40% increase in total output (E1, E10, E16, E22). Support capacity is set by total tickets handled against demand, so total output, not output per hour, is the operative metric (E5).
criteriaAssessments.mechanisms: Shorter weeks raise output per hour through less fatigue, fewer low-value meetings and more intense work, but this mostly offsets the lost hours rather than adding net capacity. In support, part of the work is reactive and arrives at fixed times, which limits how much intensity can compensate.
strengths: Across the pooled sample, the CI rules out a 40% gain in total output (E2)
weaknesses: No customer-service subgroup output figure is reported, so the pooled CI cannot be assumed to hold for support. The -7% lower bound is material for a coverage-bound org (E2, E3, K13)
Nordvik's baseline hours are not stated, so the 20% cut used in the per-hour arithmetic is an assumption (E5)
How 'output' was aggregated across firms is unknown (E2)

criteriaAssessments.assessment: This is the main org-specific risk. In Nordvik's customer-service teams, first-response time was 11% slower (95% CI +4% to +18%) unless schedules were staggered (E3). The size of the effect with staggering, and whether staggering was randomised, are not reported. UK pilot reports describe service-level problems in call centres, addressed through staggering or extra hiring, and note that Monday and Friday peaks limit which days can be taken off (E13). For South Cambridgeshire, contact-centre call answering is reported among the improved measures, with 22 of 24 KPIs holding or improving (E15). Against that, a minister raised concerns about fewer calls answered and fewer resolved first time (E24), and how the contact centre was rostered is undocumented (E25). The case is non-randomised and rests on search summaries. Whether this org has the SLA headroom to absorb any slowdown is unknown (E17).
criteriaAssessments.mechanisms: If everyone takes the same day off, coverage falls on that day and queues build. Even with staggering, each day has about 20% fewer agent-hours unless headcount or overtime rises, so response time depends on how close current staffing runs to demand peaks.
strengths: Support-specific, randomised and objectively measured response-time evidence (E3)
Staggering is identified as a mitigation in more than one source (E3, E13)
weaknesses: The effect size under staggering is not reported (E3)
No source has objective SLA data for staggered vs non-staggered support schedules, and the South Cambs evidence conflicts internally (E13, E15, E24, E25)
The org's SLA headroom and coverage hours are unknown (E17)

criteriaAssessments.assessment: Wellbeing gains are plausible but not established for this org. The Nordvik summary reports 'improved by 0.4 SD' on a validated burnout scale (E4). It does not say whether this is a difference between arms or a before-and-after change within the treatment arm, and it gives no CI or significance test (E18). 'Validated' describes the scale, not the finding. Fan, Schor et al., reported in Nature Human Behaviour, found burnout falling from 2.83 to 2.38 on a 1-to-5 scale in a large, controlled but non-randomised, self-reported study (E21). The UK pilot follow-up reports the gains holding at about one year (E12). Both external studies ran without pay cuts (E11, E20). The direction is consistent across sources, but none is specific to support, and the size and reliability of the effect for this org, especially under reduced pay, are uncertain.
criteriaAssessments.mechanisms: An extra recovery day reduces cumulative emotional exhaustion, which is high in support work because of repeated customer interactions. Burnout scales capture exhaustion and cynicism, which respond to recovery time. A pay cut could offset the gain through financial stress, and the evidence does not test this.
strengths: A validated measurement scale within a randomised trial (E4)
Independent evidence points the same way (E21, E11), with some durability evidence (E12)
weaknesses: No CI or significance test, the comparison basis is unclear (between arms or within arm), and the result is pooled rather than support-specific (E4, E18)
Pay terms in Nordvik are unknown, and the external positive results were at full pay (E18, E11, E20)
Novelty or Hawthorne effects cannot be excluded beyond 9 to 12 months, and the durability evidence is self-selected and self-reported (E4, E12)
If staggering raises the intensity of the remaining shifts, the wellbeing gain could shrink in support (inference from E3, E13)

criteriaAssessments.assessment: The Nordvik summary reports annualised voluntary attrition of '9.1% vs 13.0%' (E4). The arms are not labelled, and there is no CI, p-value or significance test (E18). If 9.1% is the treatment arm, the gap is 3.9 percentage points, a relative reduction of about 30% (K2). A gap of that size measured over nine months and annualised may not be statistically significant. Applied for illustration to 300 staff, it would mean about 11.7 fewer leavers a year (K10), but only if this org's attrition matched the 13.0% rate, which is unknown (E17). South Cambs reports turnover down 39%, but the figure comes from an advocate and was not verified (E15). The financial value depends on the org's cost per hire and ramp time, and on whether pay is kept (E17, E18).
criteriaAssessments.mechanisms: Lower burnout and a scarce benefit raise the cost of leaving, which cuts voluntary exits. In support, each avoided exit saves recruiting, training and ramp-up time, and fewer novice agents also helps throughput and quality. A pro-rata pay cut could have the opposite effect on exits.
strengths: Directionally supported by another, unverified case (E15)
weaknesses: No CI or significance test, unlabelled arms, and the result is pooled rather than support-specific (E4, E18)
Nine months is short for an annualised attrition estimate (E4)
No org baseline or cost-per-hire data, and pay terms are unknown (E17, E18)

criteriaAssessments.assessment: Pay terms are the deciding cost question, and none of the four supplied sources states them (E18, E19). The external trials that reported benefits kept full pay: the UK pilot's 100:80:100 model (E20), Microsoft Japan (E23), South Cambridgeshire (E24), and Fan, Schor et al. per one summary (E11). At full pay, cost per paid hour rises 25% (K12). Headcount-neutral payroll is unchanged, but any hours bought back to protect coverage cost full rates. For example, holding agent-hours constant at 32 hours would take about 375 FTE (K7), which is about 25% more payroll at full pay (K12). At pro-rata pay, payroll per head falls, but staff take a 20% pay cut (K5), and no evidence here shows that the wellbeing and attrition effects survive that. Other cost signals also apply. Varmland's milder 10% hours cut (K6) still raised overtime costs by 6% (E7), but the base pay cost is not stated (E19) and the figure is unverified (E9). At Svartedalen, about 17 extra staff were hired for about 68 nurses, roughly 25% more (K11), with a 6-hour day (E14). If the prior day was 8 hours, which E14 does not state, that is a 25% hours cut (K14). The extra staff on 6-hour days would then restore only about 94% of prior staff-hours (K15). The hiring replaced lost hours, with no productivity offset, and the city judged it too costly. UK pilot call centres sometimes had to hire extra staff (E13). If Nordvik's pooled per-hour gain transferred fully to support, holding total output at the central estimate would need about 306 staff (K8). E3 casts doubt on that transfer, so treat it as an optimistic bound. A 300-person change also involves contract amendments, the treatment of benefits and leave, employee consultation and legal review. The packet has no evidence on these, and they depend on jurisdiction. Designing rosters, setting up a control group, choosing metrics and settling pay terms all need lead time, which argues for a phased start.
criteriaAssessments.mechanisms: Coverage-bound work cannot shift demand into fewer days, so any shortfall in agent-hours at peak times is filled by overtime, new hires or slower service. Under full pay, each replacement hour costs 25% more per hour worked than before. Per-hour productivity gains help with backlog work but less with live queues.
strengths: Several analogues agree on the cost mechanism (E7, E13, E14)
Staggering is a known, low-cost first mitigation (E3, E13)
The pay terms of the external positive trials are documented, if only in search summaries (E20, E23, E24)
weaknesses: None of the four supplied sources states pay terms, so their cost and benefit figures cannot be mapped onto either pay design (E18, E19)
None of the cost analogues is a support org (E7, E14)
The Varmland figures are unverified, and Svartedalen's baseline hours are not stated (E9, E14)
The org's utilisation, coverage data and intended pay terms are absent (E17)
No evidence on contract, consultation or legal requirements

claims.text: The COO's '40%' matches a self-rated productivity figure from an uncontrolled survey of 60 engineering and design staff (Kestrel). It also matches Microsoft Japan's 39.9% year-on-year (August 2019 vs August 2018) rise in sales per employee. No comparison group is described for that figure, so 'uncontrolled' is an inference. Neither is a controlled measure of total output.

The only randomised, objectively measured source found pooled team output of -2% (95% CI -7% to +3%) across 112 teams under a 32-hour week. That interval rules out a 40% gain in total output. It is pooled with non-support work, and no customer-service subgroup output is reported, so it cannot be assumed to bound support losses. At the -7% lower bound, a 300-person org would lose about 21 FTE-equivalents of throughput.

Assuming a 40-to-32-hour cut (20%), which the source does not state, Nordvik's central estimate implies output per paid hour up about 22.5%, and about +16% to +29% across the CI. That still does not add total capacity.

In customer-service teams, first-response time was 11% slower (95% CI +4% to +18%) unless schedules were staggered, so switching the whole company to a shared day off puts service levels at material risk.

The Nordvik summary reports wellbeing 'improved by 0.4 SD' on a validated burnout scale. It gives no CI or significance test and does not say whether the figure compares arms or is a before-and-after change, so its reliability is unknown. The direction is supported by a large, controlled but non-randomised, self-reported study reported in Nature Human Behaviour, which ran without pay cuts.

The Nordvik summary reports annualised voluntary attrition of 9.1% vs 13.0%, with unlabelled arms and no CI or significance test. If 9.1% is the treatment arm, that is a relative reduction of about 30%. Applied for illustration to 300 staff at a 13.0% baseline, it would be about 11.7 fewer leavers a year. Whether the gap is statistically significant cannot be determined from the summary.

Coverage-bound services in other trials absorbed shorter hours partly through overtime or extra headcount. Varmland saw overtime up 6% from only a 10% hours cut, with base pay cost unstated. Svartedalen added about 25% more staff for a 6-hour day; if the prior day was 8 hours, that is a 25% hours cut, and the extra staff restored only about 94% of prior staff-hours, so they replaced lost hours rather than reflecting any productivity offset. Some UK pilot call centres needed extra hires.
Whether a full rollout is net positive for this org cannot be determined. Its SLA headroom, coverage hours, attrition rate, cost per hire, utilisation and intended pay terms were not supplied.

The existence, peer-review status and reported figures of the Nordvik working paper could not be checked independently, and neither could the Varmland report. The conclusions rest on the supplied summaries.

Illustrative bounds for 300 staff. Holding agent-hours constant at 32 hours would need about 375 FTE, which is about 25% more payroll at full pay. If Nordvik's pooled per-hour gain transferred fully to support, which the customer-service response-time penalty casts doubt on, holding total output at the central estimate would need about 306.

South Cambridgeshire reportedly improved contact-centre call answering under a four-day week. This conflicts with a ministerial concern about fewer calls answered, and the scheduling design behind the result is undocumented. It therefore shows at most that service can sometimes be held, not how.
Employee appetite for a four-day week is high (71% of 4,000 vendor-survey respondents say they would be more productive), but this measures attitude, not an effect.

None of the four supplied sources states pay terms. The external trials that reported wellbeing or retention benefits kept full pay (UK pilot 100:80:100, Microsoft Japan, South Cambridgeshire, and Fan et al. per one summary). Their benefits therefore do not show what a pro-rata design would produce. At full pay, cost per paid hour rises 25%.

A pilot of about 60 agents over 6 months would expect only about 3.9 leavers at a 13.0% annual rate and about 2.7 at 9.1%. Attrition therefore cannot be a go/no-go metric for the pilot. Service, throughput, cost and burnout scores can.

alternatives.option: Full company-wide rollout to all 300 staff from Q2
alternatives.comparison: This brings any wellbeing and attrition benefits (E4) to everyone soonest, but those benefits are of unknown reliability (E18). The case rests on an unsupported 40% premise (E1, E16), with no internal control. It exposes all queues to the +11% first-response risk if staggering is imperfect (E3). At full pay, any hours bought back to protect coverage cost 25% more per hour (K12, K7). At pro-rata pay, it imposes a 20% pay cut with no evidence that the benefits survive (E18, E19, E20). Contract and consultation steps for 300 staff must also be completed before Q2. It cannot be reversed cleanly and would generate no causal evidence.

alternatives.option: Randomised, staggered pilot starting in Q2 (illustratively about 60 agents in randomly assigned teams vs about 60 in control teams, at least 6 months, at the pay terms intended for any rollout)
alternatives.comparison: This tests service, throughput and cost (E3, E7) on real data, and it fills the missing baselines (E17). Randomly assigning teams rather than taking volunteers avoids bringing back the selection bias that weakens E1, E11 and E12. Attrition cannot be detected at this scale and duration (K16, K17), so it is a monitored secondary outcome, with burnout scores as the leading indicator. Costs: time, temporary inequity between teams, and overflow contamination if control teams absorb pilot queues. Decision rules are set out under practical implications.

This avoids service, cost and pay-term risk. The wellbeing and attrition gains it would forgo are reported without uncertainty measures (E4, E18), so their value is unproven rather than established. Independent evidence still points in a favourable direction (E21, E12), and staff appetite is high (E6). Rejecting the idea outright gives up the chance to test it cheaply.

alternatives.option: Milder reduction (for example 36 hours, or a 9-day fortnight)
alternatives.comparison: A 10% cut (K6), as at Varmland, still raised overtime by 6% (E7) but reportedly maintained service. It may balance coverage and wellbeing, but no source here tests its effect on support output or attrition, and Varmland's pay terms are unknown (E19).

tradeoffs: Possible wellbeing and retention gains (E4, of unknown reliability per E18) against a first-response slowdown unless staggered (E3)

Full pay keeps the conditions under which external benefits were observed (E20, E23, E24) but raises cost per paid hour 25% (K12). Pro-rata pay controls cost but moves outside any tested condition (E18, E19)
Staggering protects coverage (E3, E13) but complicates scheduling and may dilute the perceived benefit, for example when the day off is midweek rather than a Friday
Speed of rollout against quality of evidence: a Q2 company-wide start gives up the chance to measure causal impact
Possible hiring or overtime cost (E7, E14) against avoided replacement cost from lower attrition (E4). The net depends on internal figures and pay terms (E17)
edgeCasesAndFailureModes: Demand peaks on Mondays and Fridays make long-weekend patterns unworkable and push days off to midweek (E13)
Teams already running near capacity will see the slowdown turn into SLA breaches and backlog, not just slower responses (E3, E17)
Hidden overtime or after-hours work could erode both the cost case and the wellbeing gain (E7)
A 9-month novelty effect could fade, so attrition and wellbeing benefits shrink after rollout (E4, E12)
A Goodhart effect: agents might close tickets faster at the expense of resolution quality or reopen rates, inflating ticket counts while customer satisfaction falls
Contamination in a pilot, where control teams absorb overflow from pilot teams and bias the comparison
24/7 or multi-timezone queues need shift-based designs closer to Svartedalen's than an office four-day week (E14)
A pro-rata pay cut could raise attrition rather than lower it, reversing the retention case (E18, E19)

counterarguments.argument: Output per hour rises about 22.5%, so the COO is directionally right that productivity goes up.
counterarguments.response: If hours fell 20%, which is assumed rather than stated (E5), pooled per-hour productivity does rise (K1). But pooled total output is flat to slightly down (E2), support-specific output is unreported, and a support org must meet total demand, so per-hour gains do not create capacity (E5). The claimed 40% is also not that per-hour figure: it matches self-rated or sales-per-employee numbers (E1, E22).

counterarguments.argument: Many companies kept the policy after the UK pilot, which shows it works.
counterarguments.response: 89% continuing (E12) shows employers were satisfied, under full pay (E20), but says nothing about objective support throughput or SLAs. The firms were self-selected, and call centres in the same pilot reported service problems (E13).

counterarguments.argument: South Cambridgeshire improved call answering, contradicting Nordvik's response-time penalty.
counterarguments.response: This contradiction is unresolved. No source describes how the South Cambs contact centre rostered rest days (E25). A minister separately raised concerns about fewer calls answered and resolved first time (E24), which may reflect a different metric or period than E15. Reconciling it with Nordvik through staggering would be speculation. South Cambs is non-randomised and rests on search summaries, so Nordvik's randomised estimate (E3) carries more weight on the risk.

counterarguments.argument: Nordvik cannot be found, so it should be ignored.
counterarguments.response: Failing to find it in one search does not show it doesn't exist (E8). It is the supplied source with the strongest design. Its unverified status, and the gaps in its summary (E18), are why this recommendation is a pilot that generates internal evidence rather than a full commitment.

correctedUserAssumptions.assumption: 'The research is clear: a four-day week raises productivity by 40%'
correctedUserAssumptions.correction: The 40% matches a self-rated survey (Kestrel) and a one-month, year-on-year sales-per-employee comparison (Microsoft Japan, 39.9%, with no comparison group described). The randomised trial found pooled total team output of -2% (95% CI -7% to +3%), with no support-specific output figure. Output per hour was about +22.5% if hours fell 20%, which is not stated. No source shows a controlled 40% gain in total output.

correctedUserAssumptions.assumption: The evidence applies uniformly across job types, including customer support
correctedUserAssumptions.correction: Customer-service teams showed a specific penalty, with first-response time 11% slower unless schedules were staggered. Kestrel covers engineering and design staff, and Varmland made a different, milder hours change in a municipal setting.

correctedUserAssumptions.assumption: A company-wide switch from Q2 is feasible without degrading service
correctedUserAssumptions.correction: This is not supported. Without staggering, response times worsen. Coverage-bound analogues needed overtime (+6%) or extra headcount (about 25%), and call centres in the UK pilot reported service problems. At full pay, bought-back hours cost 25% more per hour. Feasibility for this org cannot be judged without its SLA, coverage data and pay terms.

calculations.purpose: Output per paid hour implied by Nordvik's central estimate (0.98 total output) with an assumed 40-to-32-hour cut
Relative reduction in annualised voluntary attrition (13.0% vs 9.1%)
Output per paid hour at the lower CI bound of total output (-7%)
Output per paid hour at the upper CI bound of total output (+3%)
Fractional hours cut from 40 to 32 hours (also the pro-rata pay cut)
Fractional hours cut in Varmland (40 to 36 hours)
FTE at 32 hours needed to keep total agent-hours equal to 300 staff at 40 hours (no productivity offset)
Headcount needed to restore total output if Nordvik's pooled central -2% applied to 300 support staff (optimistic bound)
Illustrative annual reduction in leavers for 300 staff at a 3.9 percentage-point attrition gap
Svartedalen staffing increase: about 17 extra staff over about 68 nurses
Cost per paid hour under full pay at 32 instead of 40 hours (also the payroll ratio of 375 vs 300 FTE at full pay)
FTE-equivalents of throughput lost at 300 staff at Nordvik's -7% lower CI bound
Svartedalen hours cut if the prior day was 8 hours and the trial day 6 hours (baseline assumed)
Share of prior staff-hours restored at Svartedalen: 85 staff on 6-hour days vs 68 on 8-hour days (assumed baseline)
Expected leavers among 60 pilot agents over 6 months at 13.0% annual attrition
Expected leavers among 60 pilot agents over 6 months at 9.1% annual attrition

practicalImplications: At the offsite, present the COO's 40% as an untested premise. Replace it with Nordvik's pooled, roughly flat total output (-2%, CI -7% to +3%), with no support-specific figure, and with the distinction between per-hour and total output (E2, K1, K13)

Decide pay terms (full vs pro rata) before any pilot, and run the pilot at the terms intended for rollout. Model full-pay cost per paid hour at +25% (K12) and the cost of buying back coverage hours (K7) (E18, E19, E20)
Start contract, benefits, consultation and legal review early for a change of this size. The packet gives no evidence on these, and they depend on jurisdiction

Timing: use Q2 to collect baselines and launch the pilot rather than the rollout. Baselines are SLA headroom, coverage hours by channel, current attrition, cost per hire and ramp time, and utilisation vs demand (E17). Make a scale-up decision after at least 6 months of pilot data
Selection: randomly assign teams within comparable queues to pilot or control. Do not use volunteers. Protect control teams from absorbing pilot overflow
Design pilot rosters around staggered days off, with no shared Friday, and avoid Monday and Friday peaks (E3, E13)

Pre-register go/no-go rules relative to control teams. Suggested starting points for leadership to calibrate against internal SLAs: stop or redesign if pilot first-response time or SLA attainment stays outside the org's SLA headroom for two consecutive weeks; overtime above a ceiling set in advance (Varmland's +6% from a milder cut is a reference, E7); or tickets resolved per team, reopen rate or CSAT materially worse than control. Scale up only if service and throughput hold within the thresholds and the full cost at the chosen pay terms is covered by budget
Treat burnout scores as the leading wellbeing indicator and monitor attrition, but do not gate the decision on attrition: a pilot this size cannot detect it (K16, K17)
After the pilot, if the rules are met, scale up in randomly ordered waves (a stepped rollout), so each wave keeps producing causal evidence
Treat staff appetite (E6) as a recruitment and retention signal, not as evidence of productivity
remainingUncertainty: Whether the Nordvik working paper exists and reports these figures as summarised. Its peer-review status, pre-registration, contamination checks and pay terms are also unknown (E8, E18)
Whether Nordvik's 0.4 SD wellbeing figure compares arms, which attrition arm is which, and whether either result is statistically significant (E18)
The size of Nordvik's response-time effect under staggered schedules, and whether staggering was randomised or self-selected (E3)
Output, wellbeing and attrition results for the customer-service subgroup specifically (E2, E4)
Whether the wellbeing and attrition effects last beyond 9 to 12 months (E4, E12)
The org's own SLA headroom, attrition baseline, cost per hire, utilisation and intended pay terms (E17)
Whether the benefits would carry over under a pro-rata pay cut: no source tests this (E18, E19, E20)
Contract, consultation and legal requirements for the change: not covered by the packet
Whether the Varmland figures are accurate, how the 6% overtime increase was measured, and what pay terms applied (E9, E19)
Svartedalen's baseline daily hours, which K14 and K15 assume to be 8 (E14)
How the South Cambridgeshire contact centre was rostered, and which call metric improved vs declined (E24, E25)
Which source the COO's 40% actually comes from (E16)
furtherResearchThatCouldChangeConclusion: Getting the full Nordvik paper. A large response-time penalty even with staggering, or a non-significant between-arm wellbeing or attrition effect, would argue against proceeding. A near-zero penalty with staggering, stable subgroup output and significant between-arm benefits would strengthen the case for a faster rollout
